prompt: Two switches are joined by two cables, spanning tree is on, and there is no link aggregation. What does the second cable do?
hint: Lesson 20's triangle had a spare too.

choices.text: Carries half the traffic
choices.why: That is what aggregation adds. Spanning tree sees two paths and keeps one.

choices.text: Starts a broadcast storm
choices.why: A storm needs spanning tree off. Here it is on.

choices.text: Sits blocked until the first one fails
choices.why: Right, and then it takes listening and learning before it forwards.

choices.text: Carries broadcasts while the first carries the rest
choices.why: Spanning tree blocks a port for broadcasts as well as the rest.

prompt: At the start of the lab, sw1's e1 and e2 are UP with LOWER_UP, yet pc1's ping to pc2 loses 1 of 1. Why?
hint: A signal is not the same as a path through the switch.

choices.text: The cables are crossed, e1 on one end meeting e2 on the other
choices.why: The lab cables e1 to e1 and e2 to e2, and a crossed pair would still carry frames.

choices.text: Neither cable is part of a bridge yet
choices.why: Right. sw1 forwards nothing onto them until the bond joins br0.

choices.text: Spanning tree is blocking one of them and the other is listening
choices.why: Spanning tree is not part of this lab, and a listening port would recover by itself.

choices.text: pc2 has no address yet
choices.why: pc2 is 10.20.10.22 from the start, and the same ping works once the bond is up.

prompt: Match each system to what it calls link aggregation.
hint: One idea, four names.

prompt: Linux names the LACP mode 802.3ad. Which IEEE standard holds LACP today?
hint: It moved out of 802.3 into the 802.1 family.

choices.why: That is spanning tree, lesson 20.
Right. 802.3ad was where it was first published.
That is VLAN tagging, lesson 19.
That is the first PoE standard.

prompt: In /proc/net/bonding/bond0 on sw1, both members list the partner system MAC 02:fc:ce:91:32:14. What does that confirm?
hint: Whose MAC is it, and why does it matter that it is the same twice?

choices.text: Both cables carry the same frames, one copy each
choices.why: A LAG puts each frame on one member. The MAC identifies the far switch, not the traffic.

choices.text: sw1 is the partner of itself
choices.why: sw1's own system MAC is 02:1d:22:fd:7e:72, listed as the actor.

choices.text: Both cables were given the same MAC by the administrator
choices.why: The bond copies e1's MAC onto its members; the partner MAC comes from sw2's LACPDUs.

choices.text: Both cables lead to one switch, sw2
choices.why: Right. That is the check a static LAG never makes.

prompt: Each member of the bond reports port state: 63, a byte in which each flag is one bit. How many flags are set?
hint: Write 63 in binary.

prompt: One cable of a two-cable LAG is plugged by mistake into a different switch. What does LACP do that a static LAG does not?
hint: Each LACPDU says who sent it.

choices.text: Sends half the traffic to the wrong switch
choices.why: That is the static LAG's behaviour, which trusts its own configuration.

choices.text: Sees a different partner on that cable and leaves it out of the bundle
choices.why: Right. A port joins only when its partner agrees to the same group.

choices.text: Blocks the cable with spanning tree
choices.why: Spanning tree sees one logical port. Keeping members in or out is LACP's job.

choices.text: Shuts both cables until the mistake is fixed
choices.why: The correctly plugged cable keeps working on its own.

prompt: In /proc/net/bonding/bond0 the end you are reading on is the actor, and the far end of each cable is the ___.
hint: Its MAC, its key, its port state.

prompt: Before the pings, sw1's e1 had sent 25 packets; after them, 158. How many frames did e1 send during the test?
hint: After minus before.

prompt: Why does a LAG not simply send frames down its cables in turn, one each?
hint: Think of two frames of the same TCP connection.

choices.text: Frames of one conversation would arrive out of order
choices.why: Right. Hashing keeps a conversation on one member, so its frames stay in sequence.

choices.text: The switch at the other end would see the same MAC address on two ports and flap
choices.why: Both members belong to one logical port, so the far switch learns the MAC on bond0, not on a member.

choices.text: LACP forbids it by design to save processing time
choices.why: Spreading by turns is cheaper to compute. The objection is ordering, not cost.

choices.text: Round-robin would make spanning tree block a member
choices.why: Spanning tree sees bond0 as one port whatever happens inside it.

prompt: Two servers are joined through a LAG of two 10 Gb/s members with xmit_hash_policy layer3+4. A backup copies one file over one TCP connection. What is the most it can reach?
hint: layer3+4 spreads connections. How many are there?

choices.text: 20 Gb/s, since layer3+4 uses the ports as well as the addresses
choices.why: The ports spread different connections. This one keeps its ports and so keeps its member.

choices.text: 5 Gb/s, since each member is shared
choices.why: No other traffic crosses the LAG here, so the member is not shared.

choices.text: 20 Gb/s once LACP rebalances it
choices.why: LACP decides membership; it does not split one conversation across members.

choices.text: 10 Gb/s, the speed of one cable
choices.why: Right. One conversation stays on one member.

prompt: Match each Linux transmit hash policy to what it hashes.
hint: The number says which layers go in.

prompt: sw1's two members together sent 220 more frames during a test of 150 pings from pc1. Which of these are counted in that 220? Choose all that apply.
hint: These are sw1's transmit counters.

choices.text: The 150 echo requests on their way to sw2
choices.why: Yes, they leave sw1 over the bond.

choices.text: LACPDUs, one a second on each member
choices.why: Yes. The fast rate keeps them coming during the 30 seconds.

choices.text: The 150 echo replies on their way back to pc1
choices.why: Replies arrive at sw1. They are on sw2's transmit counters.

choices.text: The frames pc1 sent to sw1 on port p1
choices.why: That is sw1's p1, receiving. The counters read are e1 and e2.

prompt: pc1 pinged pc3 20 times while e1 was pulled, and 20 replies came back. Why does that not prove the bond moved traffic from e1 to e2?
hint: Which cable were those pings on?

choices.text: The ping ran on sw2, which has no bond
choices.why: The ping ran on pc1, and sw2 had the same bond configured.

choices.text: Twenty pings are too few to measure anything
choices.why: Twenty is enough to see a 30-second outage like lesson 20's. The question is which cable they used.

choices.text: MII Status for e1 still said up
choices.why: It said down. That part of the failover is in the capture.

choices.text: The hash could have put them on e2 from the start
choices.why: Right. Then pulling e1 did not touch them. What the capture does show is bond0 staying up.

prompt: With lacp_rate fast, a member is taken out after missing three LACPDUs in a row. About how many seconds is that?
hint: Fast means one a second.

prompt: A media converter in the middle of a LAG member fails. The switch port's link light stays on. What notices?
hint: The signal is still there; something else stops.

choices.text: miimon, within 100 ms
choices.why: miimon watches the carrier, and the carrier is still there.

choices.text: Spanning tree, after max age
choices.why: Spanning tree sees bond0, not the members inside it.

choices.text: LACP, when the partner's LACPDUs stop arriving
choices.why: Right, about three seconds at the fast rate.

choices.text: The PCs, as soon as their pings start timing out
choices.why: Pings might show a loss, but the bond keeps using a dead member unless LACP removes it.

prompt: To make a bond report itself down when fewer than two members are up, its ___ setting goes from 0 to 2.
hint: The previous section's output listed it at 0.

prompt: Match each PoE standard or type to the power it guarantees at the switch port.
802.3af supplies 15.4 W at the switch port and promises 12.95 W at the device. How many watts does the standard allow the cable to lose?
hint: Port minus device.

prompt: A laptop is plugged into a port of an 802.3af switch. Why does it not receive power?
hint: The switch checks before it powers anything.

choices.text: It does not present the 25 kΩ signature, so the switch applies no power
choices.why: Right. Detection comes before power.

choices.text: PoE power flows on pairs a laptop does not use
choices.why: A gigabit laptop uses the four pairs; the protection is detection, not wiring.

choices.text: Laptops ask for class 0, which means no power
choices.why: Class 0 is a PD that announces no class, and it gets the Type 1 maximum.

choices.text: Its network card blocks the voltage with a fuse
choices.why: No fuse is involved; the switch decides not to power the port.

prompt: Why does this lesson show no terminal output for PoE?
hint: Think about what the lab is made of.

choices.text: Linux has no PoE commands
choices.why: Linux reads PoE status on hardware that supports it. The lab has no such hardware.

choices.text: PoE is a Cisco feature
choices.why: PoE is an IEEE standard used by many vendors.

choices.text: A virtual cable carries frames and no electricity
choices.why: Right. The lab is namespaces on one computer.

choices.text: The PoE budget of the lab's switches was set to 0 W
choices.why: There is no budget to set; the lab's switches are Linux bridges with no power hardware.

prompt: In PoE, the switch or injector that supplies the power is called the ___ (power sourcing equipment).
hint: Three letters; the device at the far end is the PD.

prompt: Put the steps a standard PoE port goes through in order, from cable plugged in to power removed.
hint: Nothing is powered before it has been found.
items: Power removed when the device is unplugged
trap: Classification before detection is the usual slip: the switch first has to know a PD is there at all.

prompt: How many watts would 24 ports need to give each one the 802.3af maximum of 15.4 W at the port?
A switch has a 370 W PoE budget and reserves power by class. How many 802.3at devices at 30 W each can it power at once?
hint: Divide and round down: a device gets its whole reservation or none.

prompt: The plan was 10 phones at class 2 (7 W), 6 access points at 30 W and 2 cameras at 60 W: 370 W. If the phones announced class 0 instead, how many watts would the plan reserve?
hint: Class 0 gets the Type 1 maximum.

prompt: A PoE switch with port priorities set runs short of budget when one more device is plugged in. What happens?
hint: The budget is a total; something has to give.

choices.text: The switch reboots to recalculate the budget
choices.why: Running short is not a crash. The switch keeps forwarding.

choices.text: Each port's power drops a little so the total fits
choices.why: Ports get their whole reservation or are left unpowered; the switch does not ration them.

choices.text: The newest device wins, as the most recent request
choices.why: Arrival order is not the rule here. The priorities that were set decide.

choices.text: The lowest-priority ports lose power
choices.why: Right. Deciding those priorities in advance is the plan.

prompt: You need both cables between two switches to carry traffic at the same time. Which arrangement does that?
hint: Lesson 20 or lesson 21?

choices.text: A LAG with LACP
choices.why: Right. Spanning tree sees one port, and the hash spreads conversations over both.

choices.text: Two plain cables with spanning tree on
choices.why: Spanning tree keeps one of them blocked as a spare.

choices.text: Two plain cables with spanning tree off
choices.why: That is a loop, and the storm from lesson 20.

choices.text: Two plain cables with RSTP instead of STP
choices.why: RSTP converges faster, but it still blocks the redundant cable.

prompt: Put the steps that built the bond on sw1 in order.
hint: The bond exists before anything joins it.
items: Make e1 and e2 members of bond0
Put bond0 in br0 and bring it up
trap: Putting the cables in br0 directly, instead of bond0, gives two plain cables between two switches: the loop of lesson 20.

prompt: A 48-port switch has a 740 W PoE budget. How many ports can it give the full 802.3at 30 W at once?
hint: Divide, then round down.
